Support servo commands sent by client

Servo commands can now be passed to the device from the home webpage,
using the arrow keys. These commands are sent as POST requests, which
isn't ideal, but is good enough for an initial implementation of the
functionality.

Eventually this should be refactored to use websocket commands instead.

Finish basic servo controls

Wraps up preliminary implementation of user provided servo commands. The
intent is that the keyup and keydown presses will send a json string to
the server, which can be parsed into a simple struct and used to command
the motors.

Uses two functions, servo_control and send_command, which determine the
servo state and send the correct value to the gpio daemon respectively.

Refactor project from webrtc+h264 to mjpeg streaming

Ultimately this project has always been overly complicated. Every
iteration up to this point has been a vain attempt to create an
interesting DIY project that is easy enough for beginners but reliable
for every day use. The Python implementation (and by extension the
partially complete Ruby impelmentation) both suffered from relying on
WebRTC streaming via Janus for the core video streaming functionality.
This has been enough of an issue with cross-browser compatibility that I
eventually gave up on the project altogether, which is unfortunate.

The new project direction will be focused solely on MJPEG streaming,
which should be supported by all browsers, and might even allow me to
make a simple mobile app for controlling the rover. The idea of being
able to finally bring the project to (what I consider) completion is
fairly exciting, and I am looking forward to how it progresses from
here.

tl;dr
Python -> Ruby -> Rust
WebRTC/Janus/Gstreamer -> mjpeg raspivid
Clunky, must use X browser on X device for this to work -> fully
operational on all devices

Refactor project from python to ruby

This project has been stale for a while, which is largely due to a
number of poor decisions made when developing the project. Namely:
- The user creation process was overly complicated
- The project had an unconventional python set up that was unnecessarily
compensated for in the setup script
- The run script was fairly clunky
- There was no testing of any kind
- The backend mostly just consisted of a single "god file", and relied
heavily on third party libraries, which were imported haphazardly

All of these and more are fixed with this refactor, which will hopefully
allow me to revisit this project and give it more attention. The code is
a lot simpler now, and has a fair amount of testing to ensure that basic
functionality and routing works as expected. It will probably never be
able to test the GPIO functionality (since that's hard to do without a
physical device) and the video streaming functionality (since a lot of
that is reliant on Janus).

Eventually this could be expanded on to also run the setup script, once
that has been updated to not have any need for user interaction.

The previous python implementation will be frozen into branch "python".

For anyone curious about this refactoring, feel free to reach out to me
to learn more. I'm also planning on writing a blog post about my
reasoning behind the language change.

Implement color picker [skip ci]

Adds a color picker to the TUI when a reference image is provided. This
works by tracking X and Y coordinates within the image and overlaying a
"cursor" over the drawn image pixels. The color beneath the cursor in
the color picker can be used for whichever theme color is currently
active (i.e. background, foreground, function, etc).

This performs bounds checking against min x/y (0) but not the max image
dimensions, meaning the cursor can leave the image. Not sure if that's
worth fixing since it should be pretty obvious to the user what happened
to the cursor.

Use `gamut` for random theme gen, add mono theme gen [skip ci]

Switches to using the PastelPaletteGenerator from `gamut` for random
theme generation, which seems to look a lot better with a lot less logic
for modifying the palette after generation.

Adds a monochromatic theme generator, which can optionally take a
"seed" color to generate the theme. If no color is provided, it takes a
random color from gamut's HappyPaletteGenerator and uses that to
generate a monochromatic theme.

Gamut can also be used to determine if the foreground color in the form
color inputs should be white/black, rather than manually checking the
Hsv value of each color (which is what gamut is doing under the hood
anyways, but this reduces the amount of logic in form generation for
colorstorm).
Add 256 color and treesitter support for vim and neovim themes
